context: Anaxagoras made nous the cosmic mind that set the world in order. For Aristotle it is the highest power of the soul, the direct grasp of first principles, and the activity of the divine unmoved mover, which thinks only itself: thinking of thinking.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: ἔστιν ἡ νόησις νοήσεως νόησις
quote.translation: its thinking is a thinking of thinking.

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean: each virtue lies between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage sits between rashness and cowardice. The mean is 'relative to us', fixed by practical wisdom, not an arithmetical midpoint.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: μεσότης τις ἄρα ἐστὶν ἡ ἀρετή, στοχαστική γε οὖσα τοῦ μέσου
quote.translation: Virtue, then, is a kind of mean, since it aims at what is intermediate.

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

translation: lack of self-control, weakness of will
context: How can someone know what is best and still do worse? Socrates denied it was possible: wrongdoing is ignorance. Aristotle answered that the akratic person knows in a way but not in the way that governs action, as a drunk may recite verses he does not understand.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: τῶν περὶ τὰ ἤθη φευκτῶν τρία ἐστὶν εἴδη, κακία ἀκρασία θηριότης
quote.translation: of the things to be avoided in character there are three kinds: vice, lack of self-control, brutishness.

image.credit: After Lysippos · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: For Homer the psychē is the breath-soul that leaves at death. Socrates made care of the psychē the whole task of life; Plato divided it into reason, spirit and appetite. Aristotle defined it as the form of a living body, so plants have souls too.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: φρονήσεως δὲ καὶ ἀληθείας καὶ τῆς ψυχῆς ὅπως ὡς βελτίστη ἔσται οὐκ ἐπιμελῇ οὐδὲ φροντίζεις;
quote.translation: but for wisdom and truth, and for how your soul may be as good as possible, you do not care or give a thought?

image.credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Parmenides set the 'way of truth' against the 'opinions of mortals'. Plato's divided line puts doxa below knowledge: it concerns the changing world of the senses and may be true, but cannot give its reasons. The word also meant 'glory'.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: οὔτε ἄρα ἄγνοια οὔτε γνῶσις δόξα ἂν εἴη;
quote.translation: Then opinion would be neither ignorance nor knowledge?

image.credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Sōphrosynē is self-knowledge and self-control together: the harmony in which reason rules and the desires agree. In the Republic it is the virtue by which the parts of the soul, and the classes of the city, agree about who should rule.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Perseus Digital Library (PerseusDL canonical-greekLit)

quote.text: κόσμος πού τις, ἦν δ' ἐγώ, ἡ σωφροσύνη ἐστὶν καὶ ἡδονῶν τινων καὶ ἐπιθυμιῶν ἐγκράτεια
quote.translation: Temperance, I said, is a kind of order, a mastery of certain pleasures and desires.

image.credit: Marie-Lan Nguyen · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Anselm's motto: the believer does not reason in order to believe but believes and then seeks to understand. His Proslogion, originally titled with this phrase, contains the ontological argument: God is that than which nothing greater can be thought.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against The Latin Library

quote.text: ut prius Exemplum meditandi de ratione fidei, et sequens Fides quaerens intellectum diceretur
quote.translation: that the first should be called 'An Example of Meditating on the Reason of Faith' and the next 'Faith Seeking Understanding'.

image.credit: Mum's taxi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

translation: I believe so that I may understand
context: Anselm's companion formula to fides quaerens intellectum, echoing Augustine: understanding is the reward of faith, not its precondition. It sums up the early scholastic view of the relation between reason and revelation.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against The Latin Library

quote.text: Neque enim quaero intelligere ut credam, sed credo ut intelligam.
quote.translation: For I do not seek to understand so that I may believe; I believe so that I may understand.

image.credit: Mum's taxi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Can we speak of God at all? Aquinas holds that 'good' or 'wise' said of God and of creatures is neither univocal (same meaning) nor equivocal (unrelated): it is analogical, grounded in creatures' likeness to their cause. Scotus argued instead for univocity.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Corpus Thomisticum (corpusthomisticum.org, Leonine text)

quote.text: Et iste modus communitatis medius est inter puram aequivocationem et simplicem univocationem.
quote.translation: And this mode of community lies midway between pure equivocation and simple univocity.

image.credit: Carlo Crivelli · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

translation: entities are not to be multiplied
context: The principle of parsimony known as Ockham's razor: do not posit more things than needed to explain the facts. This exact Latin wording is a later formulation (John Punch, 1639); Ockham's own versions read 'plurality is not to be posited without necessity'.
attribution_note: Quote checked against archive.org scan (OCR, fuzzy-matched): https://archive.org/details/william-of-ockham-opera-philosophica-vol-2

quote.text: ipsa substantia sine omni alia re absoluta, totaliter distincta, formaliter inhaerente, est quanta et corpus. Igitur superfluum est talem rem aliam ponere sibi inhaerentem.
quote.translation: substance itself, without any other absolute thing wholly distinct from it and formally inhering in it, is quantified and a body. So it is superfluous to posit such another thing inhering in it.

image.credit: self-created (Moscarlop) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Do 'humanity' or 'redness' exist apart from individual humans and red things? Realists said yes; nominalists like Ockham said universals are only names or concepts. The medieval quarrel over universals began with Boethius' Latin commentary on Porphyry.
attribution_note: Quote checked against archive.org scan (OCR, fuzzy-matched): https://archive.org/details/aniciimanliiseue48boet (CSEL 48)

quote.text: ipsa enim genera et species subsistunt quidem alio modo, intelleguntur uero alio, et sunt incorporalia, sed sensibilibus iuncta subsistunt in sensibilibus
quote.translation: genera and species themselves subsist in one way but are understood in another; they are incorporeal, yet, joined to sensible things, they subsist in sensible things.

image.credit: self-created (Moscarlop) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

translation: innate grasp of moral first principles
context: Aquinas distinguishes synderesis, the natural habit by which we know the first principles of practical reason, such as 'good is to be done and evil avoided', from conscientia, applying them to particular acts. The word comes from a garbled Greek term in Jerome.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Corpus Thomisticum (corpusthomisticum.org, Leonine text)

quote.text: synderesis dicitur instigare ad bonum, et murmurare de malo
quote.translation: synderesis is said to urge us toward good and to murmur against evil.

image.credit: Carlo Crivelli · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Genesis says humans were made in the image of God. Augustine located the image in the mind's trinity of memory, understanding and will; Aquinas in the rational soul. The idea grounded medieval and later claims about human dignity.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against augustinus.it (Latin text)

quote.text: Ecce ergo mens meminit sui, intellegit se, diligit se: hoc si cernimus, cernimus trinitatem; nondum quidem Deum, sed iam imaginem Dei.
quote.translation: See, then: the mind remembers itself, understands itself, loves itself. If we discern this, we discern a trinity: not yet God, but already the image of God.

image.credit: Philippe de Champaigne · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Writing after the sack of Rome in 410, Augustine describes two cities formed by two loves: love of self to the contempt of God, and love of God to the contempt of self. History is the story of their mingling until the end of time.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against The Latin Library

quote.text: Fecerunt itaque ciuitates duas amores duo, terrenam scilicet amor sui usque ad contemptum Dei, caelestem uero amor Dei usque ad contemptum sui
quote.translation: two loves made two cities: the earthly by love of self to the contempt of God, the heavenly by love of God to the contempt of self.

image.credit: Philippe de Champaigne · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Spinoza defines a cause of itself as that whose essence involves existence: it cannot be conceived except as existing. Only the one substance, God, is causa sui. Nietzsche later mocked the idea.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against The Latin Library

quote.text: erit itaque causa sui id est (per definitionem 1) ipsius essentia involvit necessario existentiam sive ad ejus naturam pertinet existere.
quote.translation: It will therefore be cause of itself, that is (by Def. 1), its essence necessarily involves existence, or existence belongs to its nature.

image.credit: anonymous · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: For Spinoza the highest kind of knowledge grasps things not as they exist at a given time and place but as following necessarily from God's nature. Seen this way the mind finds a joy and freedom that do not depend on duration. Wittgenstein used the phrase in the Tractatus.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against The Latin Library

quote.text: Quicquid mens sub specie æternitatis intelligit, id ex eo non intelligit quod corporis præsentem actualem existentiam concipit
quote.translation: Whatever the mind understands under the aspect of eternity, it understands not from conceiving the body's present actual existence

image.credit: anonymous · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: The culmination of Spinoza's Ethics: the joy that comes from understanding things through God, the eternal cause of everything. It is not love of a person who loves back, but the mind's eternal part delighting in knowledge. In it lies blessedness.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against The Latin Library

quote.text: Amor Dei intellectualis qui ex tertio cognitionis genere oritur, est æternus.
quote.translation: The intellectual love of God, which arises from the third kind of knowledge, is eternal.

image.credit: anonymous · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Since monads have no windows, they cannot act on one another. Yet mind and body, and all monads, seem to interact. Leibniz's answer: God set them up so their inner states correspond perfectly, like clocks keeping identical time without any connection.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 17641 (1909 ed.)

quote.text: L'âme suit ses propres loix, et le corps aussi les siennes; et ils se rencontrent en vertu de l'harmonie préétablie entre toutes les substances
quote.translation: The soul follows its own laws and the body its own; and they agree by virtue of the harmony pre-established among all substances.

image.credit: Christoph Bernhard Francke · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Leibniz's principle that nothing happens without a reason why it is so and not otherwise. With the principle of contradiction it is one of the two great principles of reasoning. It leads him to God as the sufficient reason of the whole series of things.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 17641 (1909 ed.)

quote.text: nous considérons qu'aucun fait ne saurait se trouver vrai ou existant, aucune énontiation véritable, sans qu'il y ait une raison suffisante pourquoi il en soit ainsi et non pas autrement
quote.translation: we hold that no fact can be true or existent, no statement true, unless there is a sufficient reason why it is so and not otherwise.

image.credit: Christoph Bernhard Francke · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

translation: the best of all possible worlds
context: Leibniz argued that a perfectly good, wise and powerful God must have created the best possible world, evils included. Voltaire's Candide ridiculed the thesis through Dr Pangloss after the Lisbon earthquake of 1755.
attribution_note: Quote checked against archive.org scan of the 1912 Hachette text (OCR, fuzzy-matched)

quote.text: s'il n'y avait pas le meilleur (optimum) parmi tous les mondes possibles, Dieu n'en aurait produit aucun.
quote.translation: if there were not a best (optimum) among all possible worlds, God would not have produced any.

image.credit: Christoph Bernhard Francke · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

learn_more.label: Leibniz on the problem of evil

context: Rousseau distinguishes the general will, which aims at the common good, from the 'will of all', a mere sum of private interests. In the Social Contract legitimate law expresses the general will, and whoever refuses to obey it 'will be forced to be free'.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against French Wikisource (1762 edition)

quote.text: Chacun de nous met en commun sa personne & toute sa puissance sous la suprême direction de la volonté générale
quote.translation: Each of us puts his person and all his power in common under the supreme direction of the general will.

image.credit: Maurice Quentin de La Tour · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Rousseau separates amour de soi, natural concern for one's own preservation, from amour-propre, the self-love that depends on others' opinion and makes us compare, compete and envy. Society inflames amour-propre; his remedy is a well-ordered education and state.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against French Wikisource (1823 edition)

quote.text: L'amour-propre n'est qu'un sentiment relatif, factice et né dans la société, qui porte chaque individu à faire plus cas de soi que de tout autre
quote.translation: Amour-propre is only a relative, artificial feeling born in society, which leads each individual to value himself above everyone else.

image.credit: Maurice Quentin de La Tour · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Hobbes' description of the state of nature: without a common power to keep them in awe, humans live in a condition of war of every one against every one, and life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. Only an absolute sovereign brings peace.
attribution_note: Quote checked against archive.org scan of the 1742 edition (OCR, fuzzy-matched)

quote.text: conditionem hominum extra societatem civilem (quam conditionem appellare liceat statum naturae) aliam non esse quam bellum omnium contra omnes
quote.translation: the condition of men outside civil society (which we may call the state of nature) is nothing other than a war of all against all.

image.credit: John Michael Wright · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

translation: to be is to be perceived
context: Berkeley's immaterialism: for sensible things, existing just is being perceived. There is no matter behind our ideas. Objects persist when no human looks because God always perceives them.

source.work: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge

attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 4723

quote.text: Their ESSE is PERCIPI, nor is it possible they should have any existence out of the minds or thinking things which perceive them.
quote.translation: (Original English; capitals mark Berkeley's italics.)

image.credit: John Smibert · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Kant distinguishes a negative sense, a thing insofar as it is not an object of our sensible intuition, from a positive sense, an object of an intellectual intuition we do not have. Only the negative concept is legitimate: it marks the limit of knowledge.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 6343 (modernised spelling)

quote.text: Wenn wir unter Noumenon ein Ding verstehen, so fern es nicht Objekt unserer sinnlichen Anschauung ist, indem wir von unserer Anschauungsart desselben abstrahieren; so ist dieses ein Noumenon im negativen Verstande.
quote.translation: If by noumenon we understand a thing insofar as it is not an object of our sensible intuition, abstracting from our way of intuiting it, this is a noumenon in the negative sense.

image.credit: Johann Gottlieb Becker (1720-1782) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: When reason tries to know the world as a whole, it proves contradictory theses equally well: the world has a beginning in time, and it has none; there is freedom, and everything is causally determined. Kant's resolution: the arguments mistake appearances for things in themselves.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 6343 (modernised spelling)

quote.text: Den Zustand der Vernunft bei diesen dialektischen Schlüssen, werde ich die Antinomie der reinen Vernunft nennen.
quote.translation: The state of reason in these dialectical inferences I shall call the antinomy of pure reason.

image.credit: Johann Gottlieb Becker (1720-1782) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Instead of assuming that our knowledge must conform to objects, Kant proposes that objects must conform to our knowledge, just as Copernicus explained the heavens by moving the observer. This is why we can know some things a priori. The label is later; Kant himself compares his method to Copernicus' 'first thoughts'.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 6343 (modernised spelling)

quote.text: Es ist hiermit ebenso, als mit den ersten Gedanken des Kopernikus bewandt
quote.translation: It is just the same here as with the first thoughts of Copernicus.

image.credit: Johann Gottlieb Becker (1720-1782) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: The faculty of thinking the particular under the universal. When the rule is given, judgement is determining; when only the particular is given and a rule must be found, it is reflecting. Kant's third Critique studies reflecting judgement in beauty and in living nature.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against korpora.org (Akademie-Ausgabe)

quote.text: Urtheilskraft überhaupt ist das Vermögen, das Besondere als enthalten unter dem Allgemeinen zu denken.
quote.translation: Judgement in general is the faculty of thinking the particular as contained under the universal.

image.credit: Johann Gottlieb Becker (1720-1782) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: A beautiful flower looks as if designed to please our faculties, yet we judge it beautiful without any concept of what it is for. Kant calls this purposiveness without a purpose: the free play of imagination and understanding.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against korpora.org (Akademie-Ausgabe)

quote.text: Das Geschmacksurtheil hat nichts als die Form der Zweckmäßigkeit eines Gegenstandes (oder der Vorstellungsart desselben) zum Grunde.
quote.translation: The judgement of taste has nothing but the form of the purposiveness of an object (or of its mode of representation) as its ground.

image.credit: Johann Gottlieb Becker (1720-1782) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Kant imagines a community of rational beings each of whom is both lawgiver and subject, treating all as ends in themselves. Morality asks us to act as if we were members of such a kingdom. In it everything has either a price or a dignity.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against korpora.org (Akademie-Ausgabe)

quote.text: ein Reich der Zwecke (freilich nur ein Ideal) heißen kann
quote.translation: can be called a kingdom of ends (admittedly only an ideal).

image.credit: Johann Gottlieb Becker (1720-1782) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Hegel's phrase for what is fully developed: no longer merely implicit (an sich) like a seed, nor just set over against itself (für sich), but explicitly what it is in itself. Spirit's journey is from an sich to an und für sich.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Projekt Gutenberg-DE

quote.text: auf ihre Erscheinung vielmehr als darauf, wie sie an und für sich ist
quote.translation: on its appearance rather than on how it is in and for itself.

image.credit: Jakob Schlesinger · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Self-consciousness, Hegel argues, exists only in being recognised by another self-consciousness. The struggle for recognition drives the lord–bondsman dialectic and, for later thinkers like Honneth, the whole of social and political life.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Projekt Gutenberg-DE

quote.text: Sie anerkennen sich als gegenseitig sich anerkennend
quote.translation: They recognise themselves as mutually recognising one another.

image.credit: Jakob Schlesinger · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: For Marx a class becomes a historical actor only when its members understand their shared interests: a class 'for itself' rather than merely 'in itself'. Lukács developed the idea in History and Class Consciousness (1923).
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against French Wikisource (1847 edition)

quote.text: Ainsi cette masse est déjà une classe vis-à-vis du capital, mais pas encore pour elle-même. Dans la lutte, … cette masse se réunit, elle se constitue en classe pour elle-même.
quote.translation: Thus this mass is already a class as against capital, but not yet for itself. In the struggle … this mass unites and constitutes itself as a class for itself.

image.credit: John Jabez Edwin Mayall · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

translation: act of thinking / what is thought
context: Husserl borrowed two Greek words to analyse every experience: the noesis is the act (perceiving, remembering, imagining), the noema the object exactly as it is meant in that act. A tree perceived and the same tree remembered share an object but differ in noema.
attribution_note: Quote checked against archive.org scan (OCR, fuzzy-matched): https://archive.org/details/jppf1.1 (Jahrbuch für Philosophie und phänomenologische Forschung I, 1913)

quote.text: Überall entspricht den mannigfaltigen Daten des reellen, noetischen Gehaltes eine Mannigfaltigkeit in wirklich reiner Intuition aufweisbarer Daten … Die Wahrnehmung z. B. hat ihr Noema
quote.translation: Everywhere the manifold data of the real, noetic content correspond to a manifold of data demonstrable in actually pure intuition … Perception, for example, has its noema.

image.credit: Unknown (Mondadori Publishers) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Sartre's formula for existentialism: a paper-knife is made to a plan, but there is no God to design human nature. We exist first and define ourselves afterwards by our choices, so we are 'condemned to be free'.
attribution_note: Short quotation (fair use) from a copyrighted work; wording checked against French Wikiquote (https://fr.wikiquote.org/wiki/Jean-Paul_Sartre), which cites the page

quote.text: L'existence précède l'essence.
quote.translation: Existence precedes essence.

image.credit: Unknown author · CC BY-SA 3.0 nl · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Heidegger pictures truth as a clearing in the forest, an open space in which beings can show themselves. Dasein stands in the clearing; it does not make it. The image replaces the Enlightenment idea of light shed by reason.
attribution_note: Short quotation (fair use) from a copyrighted work; wording checked against the Niemeyer edition of Sein und Zeit (archive.org OCR, https://archive.org/details/sein_und_zeit, fuzzy-matched)

quote.text: Es ist »erleuchtet«, besagt: an ihm selbst als In-der-Welt-sein gelichtet, nicht durch ein anderes Seiendes, sondern so, daß es selbst die Lichtung ist.
quote.translation: To say it is 'illuminated' means: lit up in itself as being-in-the-world, not by some other entity, but in such a way that it is itself the clearing.

image.credit: Willy Pragher · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Taken from Meister Eckhart, the word names for late Heidegger a calm openness toward things: using technology without being enslaved by it, saying yes and no to it at once, and waiting for meaning rather than seizing it.
attribution_note: Quote checked against archive.org scan (OCR, fuzzy-matched): https://archive.org/details/deutschemystiker02pfei (Pfeiffer, Deutsche Mystiker II, 1857)

quote.text: Der mensche, der gelâzen hât unde gelâzen ist unde nie mêr gesiht einen blik ûf daz, daz er gelâzen hât, unde stæte und unbewegt blîbet und unwandellîche in ime selber, der mensche ist alleine gelâzen.
quote.translation: The person who has let go and is let go, and never again casts a glance at what he has let go, and stays steady, unmoved and unchanging in himself: that person alone is released.

image.credit: Willy Pragher · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Baudrillard argued that in media-saturated societies signs no longer refer to a reality: they refer to other signs, producing a hyperreality more real than the real. Deleuze had used the term for copies that overturn Plato's priority of the original.
attribution_note: Short quotation (fair use) from a copyrighted work; wording checked against Simulacres et simulation, Galilée 1981 (archive.org OCR, https://archive.org/details/baudrillard-jean-1981-simulacres-et-simulation)

quote.text: Le simulacre n'est jamais ce qui cache la vérité – c'est la vérité qui cache qu'il n'y en a pas. Le simulacre est vrai.
quote.translation: The simulacrum is never what hides the truth: it is the truth that hides that there is none. The simulacrum is true.

image.credit: Ayaleila · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Derrida's practice of reading texts to show how their key oppositions, such as speech/writing or presence/absence, undo themselves: the privileged term depends on what it excludes. It is not destruction but a patient attention to what a text cannot master.
attribution_note: Short quotation (fair use) from a copyrighted work; wording checked against De la grammatologie, Minuit 1967 (archive.org OCR, https://archive.org/details/jacques-derrida-de-la-grammatologie)

quote.text: Il n'y a pas de hors-texte.
quote.translation: There is no outside-text.

image.credit: Auto-épreuve · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: An Aristotelian-scholastic word (Latin for Greek hexis) revived by Bourdieu for the embodied dispositions a social class instils: tastes, gestures and expectations that feel natural but reproduce social structures.

source.work: Esquisse d'une théorie de la pratique

attribution_note: Short quotation (fair use) from a copyrighted work; wording checked against Esquisse d'une théorie de la pratique, Droz 1972 (archive.org OCR, https://archive.org/details/pierre-bourdieu-esquisse-dune-theorie-de-la-pratique-precede-de-trois-etudes-det)

quote.text: habitus, systèmes de dispositions durables, structures structurées prédisposées à fonctionner comme structures structurantes
quote.translation: habitus: systems of durable dispositions, structured structures predisposed to function as structuring structures.

image.credit: Bernard Lambert · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Lacan's term for an excessive enjoyment that goes past the pleasure principle into pain. Barthes used it for the unsettling bliss of reading a text that breaks one's cultural assumptions, as opposed to the comfortable plaisir of the familiar.
attribution_note: Short quotation (fair use) from a copyrighted work; wording checked against Écrits, Seuil 1966 (archive.org OCR, https://archive.org/details/ecrits-jacques-lacan-1966)

quote.text: la jouissance est interdite à qui parle comme tel, ou encore qu'elle ne puisse être dite qu'entre les lignes pour quiconque est sujet de la Loi
quote.translation: jouissance is forbidden to whoever speaks as such, or else it can be said only between the lines by whoever is subject of the Law.

image.credit: Foto Moisio · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: The Tractatus opens: the world is everything that is the case, the totality of facts, not of things. Facts are combinations of objects; true propositions picture them. Wittgenstein's logical atomism shared this starting point with Russell.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 5740 (German text)

quote.text: Die Welt ist die Gesamtheit der Tatsachen, nicht der Dinge.
quote.translation: The world is the totality of facts, not of things.

image.credit: Moritz Nähr · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: The early Wittgenstein holds that the logical form of language cannot be said by propositions; it can only show itself in them. Ethics, aesthetics and the meaning of life also lie beyond what can be said. 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.'
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Project Gutenberg ebook 5740 (German text)

quote.text: Was gezeigt werden kann, kann nicht gesagt werden.
quote.translation: What can be shown cannot be said.

image.credit: Moritz Nähr · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: A group of philosophers and scientists around Moritz Schlick in 1920s Vienna, including Carnap and Neurath. Their logical positivism held that a statement is meaningful only if it can be verified empirically or is true by logic, so metaphysics is nonsense.
attribution_note: Short quotation (fair use) from a copyrighted work; wording checked against the Carnap Project transcription of the 1929 pamphlet (https://www.phil.cmu.edu/projects/carnap/editorial/latex_pdf/1929-5.pdf)

quote.text: Die wissenschaftliche Weltauffassung kennt keine unlösbaren Rätsel.
quote.translation: The scientific world-conception knows no unsolvable riddles.

image.credit: Unknown author · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Frege's 1879 formal language for pure thought, which introduced quantifiers and modern predicate logic. He aimed to show that arithmetic rests on logic alone. It is often called the most important single work in the history of logic.
attribution_note: Quote checked against archive.org scan (OCR, fuzzy-matched): https://archive.org/details/11388662 (Begriffsschrift, Halle 1879)

quote.text: Hieraus ergab sich auch der Name „Begriffsschrift".
quote.translation: Hence too the name 'concept-script'.

image.credit: Unknown author · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Look at the duck-rabbit: nothing in the drawing changes, yet suddenly you see a rabbit where you saw a duck. Wittgenstein used such 'aspect dawning' to explore how seeing is bound up with interpretation and concepts.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against The Wittgenstein Project (German text of the 1953 edition)

quote.text: Dieses Gesicht (das den Eindruck der Furchtsamkeit macht) kann ich mir auch als ein mutiges denken. … Ich rede vielmehr von einem Aspekt des Gesichtes selbst.
quote.translation: I can also think of this face (which gives an impression of timidity) as a courageous one. … Rather, I am speaking of an aspect of the face itself.

image.credit: Moritz Nähr · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: In Buddhism nirvāṇa is the extinguishing of the fires of craving, hatred and delusion, and release from the cycle of rebirth. Schopenhauer saw in it a parallel to his denial of the will; scholars still debate whether it is annihilation or ineffable peace.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against SuttaCentral (Mahāsaṅgīti Pali text)

quote.text: Yo kho, āvuso, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo—idaṁ vuccati nibbānan
quote.translation: The ending of greed, the ending of hatred, the ending of delusion: this, friend, is called nibbāna (Sanskrit nirvāṇa).

image.credit: พระมหาเทวประภาส วชิรญาณเมธี (ผู้ถ่าย-ปล่อยสัญญาอนุญาตภาพให้นำไปใช้ได้เพื่อการศึก · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: The first of the Buddha's Four Noble Truths: life as ordinarily lived is marked by duḥkha. Not just pain, but the unease of clinging to what is impermanent. Its cause is craving; its cessation is nirvāṇa; the path is the Eightfold Path.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against SuttaCentral (Mahāsaṅgīti Pali text)

quote.text: jātipi dukkhā, jarāpi dukkhā, byādhipi dukkho, maraṇampi dukkhaṁ
quote.translation: Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering.

image.credit: พระมหาเทวประภาส วชิรญาณเมธี (ผู้ถ่าย-ปล่อยสัญญาอนุญาตภาพให้นำไปใช้ได้เพื่อการศึก · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

context: In Śaṅkara's Advaita Vedānta the world of many separate things is māyā: not nothing, but an appearance superimposed on the one reality, brahman, like a rope mistaken for a snake. Schopenhauer adopted 'the veil of Maya' for the principium individuationis.

source.work: Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (a text Śaṅkara relies on)

attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against GRETIL

quote.text: māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyān māyinaṃ tu maheśvaraṃ
quote.translation: Know that nature is māyā, and the great Lord the wielder of māyā.

image.credit: Raja Ravi Varma · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Originally 'son of a lord', Confucius turned the term into a moral ideal: someone noble in character rather than birth, who cultivates humaneness and ritual propriety and is not resentful when unrecognised.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against Chinese Wikisource

quote.text: 人不知而不慍，不亦君子乎？
quote.translation: Not to be resentful when others do not recognise you: is that not to be a noble person?

image.credit: Anonymous Chinese painter of the Western Han period · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

context: Al-Ghazālī's Incoherence of the Philosophers attacked Avicenna's Aristotelian claims, such as the eternity of the world and necessary causation; fire does not burn cotton of itself, God creates the burning. Averroes replied with The Incoherence of the Incoherence.
attribution_note: Quote checked verbatim against OpenITI corpus (0505Ghazali.Tahafut)

quote.text: الاقتران بين ما يعتقد في العادة سببا وما يعتقد مسببا ليس ضروريا عندنا
quote.translation: The connection between what is customarily believed to be a cause and what is believed to be an effect is not necessary, in our view.
